Short answer: in SCOPe 2.08 the bulge domain of the V1 ATP synthase A subunit is placed in its own superfamily, b.84.5 "V1 ATP synthase A subunit, bulge domain-like" (sunid 310577), inside the fold b.84 "Barrel-sandwich hybrid" (sunid 51229). The placement says that the bulge domain has the same overall architecture as the biotinyl/lipoyl carrier domains and their relatives, but that SCOPe does NOT claim it shares a common ancestor with them. Shared superfamily is SCOPe's homology statement; shared fold alone is only a statement of structural similarity.

What the fold b.84 contains (release 2.08). The fold is described as a "sandwich of half-barrel shaped beta-sheets" and has five superfamilies: b.84.1 Single hybrid motif (sunid 51230; biotinyl/lipoyl-carrier proteins and domains, "7 to 8 strands in 2 beta-sheets"), b.84.2 Rudiment single hybrid motif (51246), b.84.3 Duplicated hybrid motif (51261; "half-barrel sheet of 8 strands sandwiched with two 3-stranded sheets"), b.84.4 Ribosomal L27 protein-like (110324; "rudiment single hybrid fold with a permuted topology"), and b.84.5 (310577). b.84.5 has a single family b.84.5.1 (sunid 310616) with two protein entries: "V1 ATP synthase A subunit, bulge domain" (sunid 310706; Thermus thermophilus HB8 domains such as d3a5ca3 = 3a5c A:113-184 and d3gqba3, plus Saccharomyces cerevisiae d3j9ta3 = 3j9t A:135-212) and "A1 ATP synthase A subunit, bulge domain" (sunid 310707; Pyrococcus horikoshii d3ikja2 = 3ikj A:114-190). The superfamily node's only annotation is a literature pointer, PubMed 19893485 (the Thermus A3B3 V1 crystal-structure paper), i.e. the superfamily was created when these V/A-ATPase structures were classified rather than by merging into an existing node.

Why it is separate from b.84.1 to b.84.4. SCOPe groups domains into one superfamily only when sequence, structural and/or functional evidence together indicate common descent. For the bulge domain none of that evidence exists: (1) no detectable sequence similarity to biotinyl/lipoyl carrier domains, the rudiment or duplicated hybrid motifs, or ribosomal L27; (2) no shared functional feature: b.84.1 domains carry a covalently attached biotin or lipoyl group on a conserved hairpin lysine and act as swinging-arm cofactor carriers, whereas the bulge is a non-catalytic insertion with no cofactor; (3) a different genomic/structural context: the bulge is an insertion of roughly 70 to 80 residues unique to V- and A-type ATPase A subunits (absent from the homologous F1 alpha and beta subunits), wedged between the N-terminal beta-barrel domain (classified in b.49.1.2) and the P-loop nucleotide-binding domain, with the C-terminal helical domain in a.69.1.2; (4) the fold-level resemblance is at the level of a small half-barrel sandwich, a simple architecture that SCOPe already subdivides into topologically distinct superfamilies (for example the permuted b.84.4), which is exactly the kind of similarity that can arise by convergence. A deterministic SCOPe comparison of d3a5ca3 (b.84.5.1) with the E. coli acetyl-CoA carboxylase biotinyl domain d1bdoa_ (b.84.1.1) returns relationship "same_fold", lowest shared node b.84, with the explicit interpretation that this is structural similarity and not by itself homology; the fold node's homology section likewise carries the warning that levels above superfamily do not imply homology.

The evolutionary claim the placement makes. Positive claim: all bulge domains in b.84.5.1 are homologous to each other, and at family level that relationship is close enough to be recognisable by sequence; this spans bacterial (Thermus), archaeal (Pyrococcus A1-ATPase) and eukaryotic (yeast V1) A subunits, consistent with the bulge having been present in the A-subunit lineage before the archaeal/eukaryotic V/A-ATPase radiation. Negative or agnostic claim: by refusing to merge b.84.5 into b.84.1 to b.84.4, SCOPe asserts that there is no adequate evidence that the bulge domain descends from the same ancestor as the biotinyl/lipoyl carrier or L27-like domains. The shared fold means only that they adopt a similar half-barrel sandwich; whether that reflects very remote divergence or independent convergence is left open. SCOPe does not assert convergence either; it simply withholds the homology claim.

Practical limits that follow. Do not transfer the cofactor-carrier function of b.84.1 domains (biotinylation/lipoylation, swinging-arm chemistry) to the bulge domain; its role in V/A-ATPases is structural and regulatory (contacting the N-terminal barrel and the B subunit), not catalytic. Do not use b.84.1 to b.84.4 structures as homology-modelling templates for the bulge domain, or vice versa; a fold-level match justifies at most a coarse topological comparison, and template-based modelling should stay inside b.84.5.1 (for example d3a5ca3, d3ikja2 or d3j9ta3). Do not treat superfamily membership as functional equivalence even within b.84.5: V1 and A1 bulge domains are homologous, but species-specific regulatory roles (such as reversible V1/Vo dissociation in eukaryotes) are not implied by the classification. Finally, representative choice matters: the Thermus entries (3a5c, 3gqb and the 9u6 series) dominate the superfamily, so sequence or structure searches seeded from them should not be read as evidence about the whole V/A-ATPase family's diversity, and any future merger of b.84.5 with another barrel-sandwich hybrid superfamily would require new evidence of shared ancestry (for example sequence-profile matches or a shared, non-trivial structural and functional motif), not just the existing fold-level resemblance.
